provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of jss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list basic technical drawing tools, explain the purpose of each tool, and demonstrate correct handling of drawing instruments.
Introduction:
Last term we studied basic technical drawing and woodwork tools. Today we will revise these important topics to build a strong foundation for this term.
Content:
Technical drawing tools include rulers, T-squares, set squares, compasses, and protractors. Each tool has a specific purpose - rulers for straight lines, T-squares for right angles, compasses for circles, and protractors for measuring angles. For example, when drawing a plan of a local market stall, we use these tools to ensure accuracy. Woodwork tools include hammers, saws, chisels, planes, and screwdrivers. Each tool must be handled carefully to prevent accidents. A carpenter building a table uses these tools to shape wood properly.
Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify and demonstrate the correct use of five technical drawing tools and five woodwork tools.
Evaluation questions:
1. Name three technical drawing tools.
2. What is the purpose of a T-square?
3. How should a chisel be held safely?
4. Why is it important to keep tools clean?
Summary:
Proper use and maintenance of technical tools is essential for accurate work and safety in the workshop.

topics.title: Technical drawing: orthographic
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain first angle projection, identify the three views in orthographic projection, and draw simple objects in first angle projection.
Introduction:
We have previously learned about basic technical drawing tools. Today we will apply these tools to create orthographic projections, which are essential in engineering drawings.
Content:
Orthographic projection is a method of representing three-dimensional objects in two dimensions. First angle projection is commonly used in Nigeria. It shows the front view, top view, and side view of an object. For example, when drawing a simple block representing a local 'suya' grill box, we show how it looks from the front, top, and side. The views are arranged with the front view in the center, top view above it, and side view to the right. All lines must be straight and measurements accurate.
Class activity:
Students will draw a simple rectangular block in first angle projection on their drawing boards using T-squares and set squares.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is orthographic projection?
2. Name the three views in first angle projection.
3. Where is the top view placed in first angle projection?
4. Why is accuracy important in technical drawing?
Summary:
First angle projection helps us accurately represent three-dimensional objects on two-dimensional paper.

topics.title: Isometric drawing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain isometric axes, construct isometric circles, and draw simple objects in isometric projection.
Introduction:
After studying orthographic projection, we now move to isometric drawing, which gives a three-dimensional view of an object on a two-dimensional surface.
Content:
Isometric drawing uses three axes at 120 degrees to each other to create a 3D effect. The isometric axes consist of vertical, 30-degree left, and 30-degree right lines. For example, when drawing a local 'koko' seller's cart, we use these axes to show how it looks in three dimensions. Circles in isometric view become ellipses, drawn using special techniques. Measurements along the axes are true length, making it easier to visualize objects.
Class activity:
Students will practice drawing a simple cube and then a rectangular box representing a local 'zobo' drink container in isometric projection.
Evaluation questions:
1. What are the angles between isometric axes?
2. How does a circle appear in isometric drawing?
3. What measurement remains true in isometric projection?
4. Name one advantage of isometric drawing over orthographic projection.
Summary:
Isometric drawing provides a clear 3D representation of objects, making it easier to visualize how things look in real life.

topics.title: Woodwork: joints
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify common wood joints, explain their uses, and demonstrate how to make a halving joint.
Introduction:
In our previous woodwork lessons, we learned about basic tools. Today we will study different types of joints used to connect pieces of wood in furniture making.
Content:
Wood joints are connections between two or more pieces of wood. Common joints include butt joint, lap joint, dovetail joint, and halving joint. Each joint has specific uses - butt joints for simple connections, lap joints for strength, dovetail joints for drawers, and halving joints for frames. For example, a carpenter making a local stool uses halving joints for the legs and seat. The halving joint is made by cutting half the depth of each piece where they meet, then joining them together with glue and nails or screws.
Class activity:
Students will practice making a halving joint using softwood pieces and basic hand tools under teacher supervision.
Evaluation questions:
1. Name three types of wood joints.
2. What is the purpose of a dovetail joint?
3. How is a halving joint made?
4. Why are joints important in woodwork?
Summary:
Properly made joints ensure strength and durability in wooden furniture and structures.

topics.title: Metalwork: marking out
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify marking out tools, explain marking out techniques, and mark out a simple template on metal.
Introduction:
We have studied wood joints in the previous lesson. Today we will learn about marking out in metalwork, which is the first step before cutting or shaping metal.
Content:
Marking out is transferring measurements to metal before cutting. Tools used include scribers, try squares, dividers, center punches, and prick punches. For example, when making a local 'yam pounder' handle, we mark out where holes will be drilled. The process involves measuring, marking lines, centering points, and making small indentations with center punches. Accuracy is crucial as even small mistakes can ruin the workpiece.
Class activity:
Students will mark out a simple template on a piece of mild steel sheet using marking out tools.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is marking out in metalwork?
2. Name three marking out tools.
3. Why is accuracy important in marking out?
4. What is the purpose of a center punch?
Summary:
Proper marking out ensures accurate cutting and shaping of metal workpieces.

topics.title: Building: foundations
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of foundations, explain their uses, and discuss factors affecting foundation choice.
Introduction:
We have studied wood and metalwork previously. Today we will learn about foundations, which are the base of any building, transferring loads from the structure to the ground.
Content:
Foundations support buildings and distribute their weight to the ground. Common types include strip foundations, raft foundations, and pile foundations. Strip foundations are used for load-bearing walls, like in our classroom building. Raft foundations spread the load over a wide area, suitable for weak soil like in some parts of Lagos. Pile foundations go deep into the ground, used for tall buildings in areas with soft soil like the Niger Delta. The choice depends on soil type, building size, and local climate.
Class activity:
Students will draw and label different types of foundations based on a classroom discussion and textbook illustrations.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of a foundation?
2. Name three types of foundations.
3. When would a pile foundation be used?
4. How does soil type affect foundation choice?
Summary:
Proper foundations are essential for the safety and stability of any building structure.

topics.title: Building: walls and floors
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify common wall and floor materials, explain different brick bonds, and discuss factors affecting material choice.
Introduction:
After learning about foundations, we now move to walls and floors, which form the main parts of building structures.
Content:
Walls and floors are major components of buildings. Common wall materials include bricks, blocks, and sandcrete. Floor materials include concrete, tiles, and wood. Brick bonds are patterns used to lay bricks for strength and appearance. Common bonds include stretcher bond, header bond, and Flemish bond. For example, the school walls use stretcher bond, where bricks are laid lengthwise. The choice of materials depends on cost, availability, climate, and intended use. In hot areas like Sokoto, thicker walls help keep buildings cool.
Class activity:
Students will draw different brick bond patterns on paper and identify which pattern is strongest for load-bearing walls.
Evaluation questions:
1. Name three wall materials.
2. What is the purpose of brick bonds?
3. Name two factors affecting material choice for walls.
4. How does climate affect building materials?
Summary:
Proper selection and construction of walls and floors ensure building durability and comfort.

topics.title: Machines: simple mechanisms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify gears and pulleys, explain their functions, and demonstrate simple mechanisms.
Introduction:
We have studied building structures. Today we will learn about simple machines and mechanisms that make work easier in our everyday lives.
Content:
Simple mechanisms are basic devices that change the magnitude or direction of force. Gears are toothed wheels that transmit motion and change speed or direction. Pulleys are wheels with grooves for ropes or belts, used to lift loads or transmit power. For example, a local grinding machine uses gears to change the speed of the grinding stone. A well uses a pulley system to lift water from deep underground. These mechanisms can be found in bicycles, cars, and even the 'okada' motorcycles we see on the streets.
Class activity:
Students will build simple gear and pulley models using kits provided to demonstrate how these mechanisms work.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is the function of a gear?
2. How does a pulley make work easier?
3. Name one place where gears are used.
4. What is mechanical advantage?
Summary:
Simple mechanisms make work easier by changing force direction or magnitude.

topics.title: Power transmission
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain belt and chain drives, identify their components, and demonstrate how they transmit power.
Introduction:
After studying simple mechanisms like gears and pulleys, we will now focus on how power is transmitted between machine parts using belts and chains.
Content:
Power transmission moves energy from one part of a machine to another. Belt drives use flexible belts on pulleys to transmit power. They are used in fans, generators, and 'agbo' grinding machines. Chain drives use chains and sprockets, found in bicycles and motorcycles. Belt drives are quieter but can slip, while chain drives are more positive but noisier. For example, a 'Danfo' bus uses a belt drive for its cooling system. The choice between belt and chain depends on the application, required power, and environmental conditions.
Class activity:
Students will assemble simple belt and chain drive models using educational kits to observe power transmission.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is power transmission?
2. Name two types of power transmission systems.
3. Compare belt drives and chain drives.
4. Where is a belt drive commonly used?
Summary:
Belt and chain drives efficiently transmit power between machine components in different applications.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer past BECE questions correctly, identify areas of weakness, and demonstrate knowledge of all topics covered this term.
Introduction:
We have completed all topics for this term. Today we will revise and practice past BECE questions to prepare for the upcoming examination.
Content:
Revision covers all topics studied this term: technical drawing, woodwork joints, metalwork marking out, building foundations and structures, and simple machines. Past BECE questions will be used to test understanding. For example, a question might ask to draw a simple isometric view of a local 'akara' seller's cart. Another question might require explaining the difference between strip and raft foundations. Students should identify areas where they need more practice and focus on those before the exam.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past BECE questions and present their answers to the class for discussion and correction.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is first angle projection?
2. Explain how to make a halving joint.
3. When would a pile foundation be used?
4. What is the difference between belt and chain drives?
5. Draw a simple isometric cube.
Summary:
Regular practice with past questions helps prepare for examinations and identifies areas needing more attention.
